Empirical Research Plan:  Compulsory Schooling, Educational Attainment, and Labor-Market Outcomes  
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
   • Primary design: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) with an Instrumental‐Variable Difference-in-Differences (IV-DiD) set-up.  
     – First stage (DiD): exploit within-state, across-cohort changes in the minimum school-leaving age (MSLA) or minimum years of compulsory schooling.  
     – Second stage: use the predicted years of schooling as the endogenous regressor for earnings (log wages) and employment.  
   • Why appropriate?  
     – Compulsory-schooling statutes changed discretely and differentially across the 48 states between 1910 and 1950, creating plausibly exogenous shifts in schooling for specific birth cohorts.  
     – Using state*cohort fixed effects in a 2SLS framework nets out common time shocks and permanent state differences, providing a clean causal interpretation.  

2. Treatment and Control  
   Treatment variable:  
     • Z_is ≡ 1 if individual i was born in state s in a cohort subject to a higher mandatory schooling requirement than the previous cohort in the same state (e.g., MSLA rises from age 14→16).  
     • Endogenous exposure: S_is = completed years of schooling.  

   Control group:  
     • Individuals born in the same state in immediately preceding cohorts (before the change) + individuals in states that do not change their law in that year.  

   Treatment timing:  
     • Event date = first cohort whose 6th birthday (or 14th birthday, depending on state statute) occurs after a law is enacted.  
     • We code “exposure” at the birth-year level so that the timing aligns with the age at which the law becomes binding.  

   (No running variable / cutoff is needed because we do not implement RDD.)  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
   A1. Relevance: Changes in MSLA raise average completed schooling.  
        – Historically verified in many settings; we test in the 1st stage.  
   A2. Excludability: MSLA affects labor-market outcomes only through schooling, not via other policy changes that differentially influence treated cohorts in treated states.  
        – Plausible because statutes targeted schooling; we bolster by controlling for contemporaneous child-labor, teacher-salary, and school-finance laws.  
   A3. Parallel Trends / Cohort Invariance: Absent the reform, outcome trends would have evolved similarly across neighboring cohorts in the same state and across states.  
        – Institutional accounts suggest no systematic anticipation; we test visually with an event-study plot of pre-trends.  
   A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-state spillovers at birth).  
        – Reasonable; migration before age 14 is limited and can be addressed by restricting to state-of-birth ≠ current-state movers.  
   A5. Monotonicity: No individual reduces schooling because the MSLA increased.  
        – Reasonable for compulsory laws that bind from below.  

4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  
   T1. Migration after birth (people born in a “treated” state may grow up elsewhere).  
        – Use state of birth not state of residence; drop those who move before age 14 where possible; test robustness to keeping migrants.  
   T2. Concurrent state-level shocks (e.g., industrialization, New Deal programs).  
        – Include state*year fixed effects, state-specific linear or quadratic trends, and controls for time-varying state characteristics (manufacturing share, unemployment).  
   T3. Manipulation of reporting (age heaping or mis-reporting schooling).  
        – Validate with digit-heaping diagnostics; re-estimate excluding heaped ages; instrument is binary so mis-measured outcome not first-stage.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ------------- 0. Packages -------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim IV
library(ggplot2)

# ------------- 1. Load Data -------------
# Assume: census_individual.csv contains one record per person
# and statutes.csv contains MSLA by state & year

dt  <- fread("census_individual.csv")
law <- fread("statutes.csv")   # columns: state, law_year, msla

# ------------- 2. Construct Variables -------------
# Merge law information
dt[, birth_year := year]  # whatever the birth-year variable is called
law[, cohort_first_exposed := law_year - msla + 6]  # age 6 entry rule
dt <- merge(dt, law[, .(state, msla, cohort_first_exposed)], 
            by.x = "state_birth", by.y = "state", all.x = TRUE)

# Instrument: treated if born in or after first exposed cohort
dt[, Z := as.integer(birth_year >= cohort_first_exposed)]

# Endogenous dosage
dt[, yrs_schooling := educ_years]

# Outcomes
dt[, ln_earnings := log(earnings)]

# Fixed-effects identifiers
dt[, cohort := birth_year]
dt[, state_cohort := interaction(state_birth, cohort)]

# Sample restriction: age 25–64, native born
dt <- dt[age %between% c(25,64) & native == 1]

# ------------- 3. Main 2SLS -------------
# First stage
fs <- feols(yrs_schooling ~ Z | state_birth + cohort, data = dt, cluster = ~state_birth)
summary(fs)

# Second stage (2SLS)
iv_main <- feols(ln_earnings ~ 1 | yrs_schooling ~ Z | state_birth + cohort, 
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state_birth)
summary(iv_main)

# Employment outcome
iv_emp  <- feols(employed ~ 1 | yrs_schooling ~ Z | state_birth + cohort, 
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state_birth)

# ------------- 4. Robustness Check: Event-Study Plot -------------
# Estimate dynamic leads/lags (placebo)
dt[, event_time := cohort - cohort_first_exposed]
es <- feols(yrs_schooling ~ i(event_time, ref = -1) | state_birth + cohort, 
            data = dt[abs(event_time) <= 10])
iplot(es) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2)
```

6. Expected Results  
   • Direction: Higher MSLA → more schooling → higher earnings and employment probability.  
   • Magnitude: Classic estimates find 0.08–0.12 log points of annual earnings per additional year of schooling; I expect 8–10 % wage increase and 1–2 pp higher employment for the marginal students induced to stay in school.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  
   C1: Instrument relevance  ………………… 1  
   C2: Instrument exogeneity ……………… 0.8 (some risk of correlated reforms)  
   C3: No direct effect (exclusion) ……… 0.7  
   C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ………… 1  
   C5: SUTVA / no spillovers ………………… 0.8  
   Overall: 4.3 / 5 → strong but must document robustness.
